lesson.title: Surviving the Crash: How Bottlenecks Reshape a Gene Pool
lesson.summary: The bottleneck effect is genetic drift triggered from the opposite direction of the founder effect: an established population suddenly and drastically shrinks, and the survivors carry forward only whatever slice of the original genetic diversity happened to make it through.
lesson.body:
Where the founder effect begins with a small group starting something new, the bottleneck effect begins with something large being suddenly cut down to a small remnant. A population that once had substantial genetic diversity, spread across many thousands of individuals, can be struck by a natural disaster, a disease outbreak, habitat loss, or intense hunting, and be reduced within a single generation to a small fraction of its former size. The individuals who happen to survive that crash are not necessarily the ones best suited to the new conditions. A wildfire, a flood, or a sudden epidemic can be just as likely to kill a genetically well adapted individual as a poorly adapted one. The alleles that make it through the bottleneck are, in large part, a matter of who happened to survive, which is exactly what makes this a form of genetic drift rather than natural selection.

Northern elephant seals provide one of the best documented examples. Hunted heavily for their blubber through the 1800s, the species was reduced to a very small number of survivors before legal protection allowed the population to recover. Today, northern elephant seals number in the tens of thousands, but genetic studies consistently find that they carry far less genetic diversity than closely related seal species that never went through such a severe crash. The population rebounded in size, but the genetic diversity lost when it bottlenecked did not simply grow back, because a bottleneck cannot recover an allele that no survivor happened to carry.

This is the key long term consequence of a bottleneck, and it is what makes the concept important beyond its historical drama: reduced genetic diversity limits a population's raw material for future evolution. A population with low variation has fewer options when a new disease, a changing climate, or a new predator appears, because natural selection can only act on variation that already exists. A bottlenecked population, even one that eventually recovers its numbers, often remains more vulnerable to extinction than a population that was never squeezed down that small, which is a major reason conservation biologists treat preserving genetic diversity, not just raw population counts, as a central goal.
